newsitem.title: CROATIA: Izetbegovic, Milosevic may meet this week - premier.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic, Milosevic may meet this week - premier.

text.p: Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic may meet Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic for U.S.-brokered talks as soon as this week, the prime minister of the Moslem-led Sarajevo government said on Tuesday.

"The meeting could materialise very soon, i.e. by the end of this week, possibly before President Izetbegovic's address to the United Nations which is scheduled for September 25," Prime Minister Hasan Muratovic said.
However, Muratovic told a news conference there was also a possibility that the meeting, arranged by U.S. peace envoy Richard Holbrooke, could be held after Izetbegovic's U.N. speech.
Holbrooke said last Sunday after separate meetings with the two leaders that he expected the talks, which would follow Bosnian elections last weekend, in about three weeks.

Speaking on a visit to Zagreb, Muratovic said the two presidents would discuss implementing the Dayton peace agreement and bilateral relations. Sarajevo and Belgrade still do not have full diplomatic relations, he said.

Muratovic, who earlier met Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, played down the possibility that Serb hardliner Momcilo Krajisnik would win most votes in the race for the three-man Bosnian presidency ahead of Izetbegovic.
"Theoretically it could also be Krajisnik from the (Bosnian) Serb Republic," he said. "But practically if the elections are correct it is hardly possible because of the electorate."
Muratovic said the Bosnian Serb Republic had an electorate of only 750,000, while the Moslems had about 900,000 votes.
Full results from the elections on Saturday have not yet been announced but voting is expected to have gone almost exclusively along ethnic lines.

Analysts say the Bosnian government is worried that former prime minister Haris Silajdzic might split the Moslem vote and allow Krajisnik to slip ahead in elections to the presidency, which will comprise a Moslem, a Serb and a Croat.
Although the three-man Bosnian presidency will rule by consensus, the candidate who wins the most votes will be the senior member who will represent the country abroad.
Muratovic said his talks with Tudjman had covered the Moslem-Croat federation, a U.S.-arranged marriage of two of Bosnia's three factions.
Powers are supposed to have transferred from the separate Croat- and Moslem-led governments to the federation but they have been delayed by bickering.
Muratovic and Tudjman also discussed the Bosnian government's Agency for Investigation and Documentation (AID). The Bosnian Croats say this is a secret police force and must be disbanded.
The other unresolved issue was the creation of a single tax authority for the federation, Muratovic added.
